docs.title: 📦 What is an Array?
docs.text: Definition: Collection of elements of the same type, stored in contiguous memory, accessed by index.

docs.title: Memory Layout
docs.text:
int arr[5] = {85, 92, 78, 95, 88};

Memory:
┌────┬────┬────┬────┬────┐
│ 85 │ 92 │ 78 │ 95 │ 88 │
└────┴────┴────┴────┴────┘
 [0]  [1]  [2]  [3]  [4]    ← indices

Address:
1000 1004 1008 1012 1016     ← each int takes 4 bytes

Key Properties:

  • Fixed size — set at declaration
  • Same type — all elements identical type
  • Contiguous — stored consecutively in memory
  • Zero-indexed — first element is index 0
  • Random access — O(1) time to access any element

docs.title: Declaration
docs.text:
type arrayName[size];

Examples:

int numbers[10];      // 10 integers
float grades[5];      // 5 floats
char name[50];        // 50 characters
double prices[100];   // 100 doubles

docs.title: Initialization
docs.text:
Method 1: Initialize all

int arr[5] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};

Method 2: Partial (rest = 0)

int arr[5] = {10, 20};  // {10, 20, 0, 0, 0}

Method 3: All zeros

int arr[5] = {0};  // All elements 0

Method 4: Inferred size

int arr[] = {10, 20, 30};  // Size is 3

Method 5: After declaration

int arr[3];
arr[0] = 10;
arr[1] = 20;
arr[2] = 30;

docs.title: ⚠️ Array Bounds
docs.text:
C does NOT check array bounds!

int arr[5];
arr[10] = 100;  // OUT OF BOUNDS! Undefined behavior!
                // May crash, corrupt data, or appear to work

Always ensure: 0 <= index < size

docs.title: 1. Linear Search
docs.text:
Find if element exists and return position.

int linearSearch(int arr[], int size, int target) {
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        if (arr[i] == target) {
            return i;  // Found at index i
        }
    }
    return -1;  // Not found
}

Time complexity: O(n)

docs.title: 3. Reverse Array
docs.text:
void reverse(int arr[], int size) {
    for (int i = 0; i < size / 2; i++) {
        int temp = arr[i];
        arr[i] = arr[size - 1 - i];
        arr[size - 1 - i] = temp;
    }
}

docs.title: 4. Copy Array
docs.text:
void copyArray(int source[], int dest[], int size) {
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        dest[i] = source[i];

}

docs.title: 5. Remove Duplicates
docs.text:
int removeDuplicates(int arr[], int size) {
    int newSize = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        int isDuplicate = 0;
        for (int j = 0; j < newSize; j++) {
            if (arr[i] == arr[j]) {
                isDuplicate = 1;
                break;
            }
        }
        if (!isDuplicate) {
            arr[newSize++] = arr[i];
        }
    }
    return newSize;
}

docs.title: Bubble Sort
docs.text:
Compare adjacent elements and swap if needed.

void bubbleSort(int arr[], int size) {
    for (int i = 0; i < size - 1; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < size - i - 1; j++) {
            if (arr[j] > arr[j + 1]) {
                // Swap
                int temp = arr[j];
                arr[j] = arr[j + 1];
                arr[j + 1] = temp;
            }
        }
    }
}

How it works: 

Pass 1: {5,2,8,1,9} → {2,5,1,8,9} (9 bubbles to end)
Pass 2: {2,5,1,8,9} → {2,1,5,8,9} (8 in place)
Pass 3: {2,1,5,8,9} → {1,2,5,8,9} (5 in place)
Done: {1,2,5,8,9}

Time complexity: O(n²)

docs.title: Selection Sort
docs.text:
Find minimum and place at front.

void selectionSort(int arr[], int size) {
    for (int i = 0; i < size - 1; i++) {
        int minIndex = i;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < size; j++) {
            if (arr[j] < arr[minIndex]) {
                minIndex = j;
            }
        }
        // Swap arr[i] with arr[minIndex]
        int temp = arr[i];
        arr[i] = arr[minIndex];
        arr[minIndex] = temp;
    }
}

Time complexity: O(n²)

docs.title: String Definition
docs.text:
In C, a string is an array of characters terminated by the null character '\0'.

char name[] = "Hello";

Memory:
┌───┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┐
│ H │ e │ l │ l │ o │ \0│
└───┴───┴───┴───┴───┴───┘
 [0] [1] [2] [3] [4] [5]

Key point: '\0' marks the end of the string!

docs.title: Why Null Terminator?
docs.text:
Functions need to know where string ends: 

// Without \0, how would printf know when to stop?
printf("%s", name);  // Prints until \0 is found

docs.title: Method 1: String Literal
docs.text:
char name[] = "Alice";
// Automatically adds \0
// Size is 6: 'A','l','i','c','e','\0'

docs.title: Method 2: Character Array
docs.text:
char name[] = {'A', 'l', 'i', 'c', 'e', '\0'};
// Must add \0 manually!

docs.title: Method 3: Specify Size
docs.text:
char name[50] = "Alice";
// Size 50, but only first 6 used
// Rest are \0

docs.title: Method 4: Character Pointer
docs.text:
char *name = "Alice";
// String literal (read-only!)
// Cannot modify: name[0] = 'B'; // ERROR!

docs.title: Output with printf
docs.text:
char name[] = "Alice";
printf("%s\n", name);        // Alice
printf("Hello, %s!\n", name); // Hello, Alice!

docs.text:
char name[50];
scanf("%s", name);  // No & needed! (array name is address)

⚠️ Problem: Stops at whitespace!

Input: "John Doe"
Result: name = "John" (stops at space!)

docs.text:

docs.title: 📚 String Library Functions
docs.text: Include: #include <string.h>

docs.title: 1. strlen() - String Length
docs.text:
Returns length without '\0'.

char str[] = "Hello";
int len = strlen(str);  // 5 (not 6!)

docs.title: 2. strcpy() - String Copy
docs.text:
char source[] = "Hello";
char dest[20];

strcpy(dest, source);  // dest = "Hello"

⚠️ Danger: No bounds checking!

char dest[5];
strcpy(dest, "Hello World");  // BUFFER OVERFLOW!

Safer: strncpy()

strncpy(dest, source, sizeof(dest) - 1);
dest[sizeof(dest) - 1] = '\0';  // Ensure null termination

docs.title: 3. strcat() - String Concatenation
docs.text:
char str1[50] = "Hello";
char str2[] = " World";

strcat(str1, str2);  // str1 = "Hello World"

⚠️ Requirements:

  • str1 must have enough space!
  • Both must be null-terminated

Safer: strncat()

docs.title: 4. strcmp() - String Comparison
docs.text:
char str1[] = "Apple";
char str2[] = "Banana";

int result = strcmp(str1, str2);
// result < 0 if str1 < str2 (Apple < Banana)
// result = 0 if str1 == str2
// result > 0 if str1 > str2

⚠️ Never use ==

if (str1 == str2)  // WRONG! Compares addresses
if (strcmp(str1, str2) == 0)  // CORRECT!

docs.text:
void my_strcpy(char dest[], char source[]) {
    int i = 0;
    while (source[i] != '\0') {
        dest[i] = source[i];
        i++;
    }
    dest[i] = '\0';  // Don't forget!
}

docs.title: 3. Manual strcmp
docs.text:
int my_strcmp(char str1[], char str2[]) {
    int i = 0;
    while (str1[i] != '\0' && str2[i] != '\0') {
        if (str1[i] != str2[i]) {
            return str1[i] - str2[i];
        }
        i++;
    }
    return str1[i] - str2[i];
}

void my_strcat(char dest[], char source[]) {
    int i = 0, j = 0;

    // Find end of dest
    while (dest[i] != '\0') {
        i++;
    }

    // Copy source to end
    while (source[j] != '\0') {
        dest[i] = source[j];
        i++;
        j++;
    }

    dest[i] = '\0';
}

Write four functions to perform basic arithmetic operations:

docs.title: Exercise 2: Prime Number Checker ⭐⭐
docs.text:
Write a function to check if a number is prime:

int isPrime(int n);  // Returns 1 if prime, 0 otherwise

Requirements:

  • Check divisibility from 2 to √n
  • Handle edge cases: n < 2 (not prime)
  • Test with: 1, 2, 7, 15, 17, 100

Expected Output:

1 is not prime
2 is prime
7 is prime
15 is not prime
17 is prime
100 is not prime
Solution 
#include <stdio.h>
#include <math.h>

int isPrime(int n);

int main() {
    int numbers[] = {1, 2, 7, 15, 17, 100};
    int size = 6;

    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        if (isPrime(numbers[i])) {
            printf("%d is prime\n", numbers[i]);
        } else {
            printf("%d is not prime\n", numbers[i]);
        }
    }

    return 0;
}

int isPrime(int n) {
    // Numbers less than 2 are not prime
    if (n < 2) {
        return 0;
    }

    // 2 is prime
    if (n == 2) {
        return 1;
    }

    // Even numbers are not prime
    if (n % 2 == 0) {
        return 0;
    }

    // Check odd divisors up to sqrt(n)
    int limit = (int)sqrt(n);
    for (int i = 3; i <= limit; i += 2) {
        if (n % i == 0) {
            return 0;
        }
    }

    return 1;
}

  • Test with: {64, 34, 25, 12, 22, 11, 90}

Expected Output:

Original array: 64 34 25 12 22 11 90
Sorted array:   11 12 22 25 34 64 90
Solution 
#include <stdio.h>

void bubbleSort(int arr[], int size);
void printArray(int arr[], int size);

int main() {
    int arr[] = {64, 34, 25, 12, 22, 11, 90};
    int size = 7;

    printf("Original array: ");
    printArray(arr, size);

    bubbleSort(arr, size);

    printf("Sorted array:   ");
    printArray(arr, size);

    return 0;
}

void bubbleSort(int arr[], int size) {
    for (int i = 0; i < size - 1; i++) {
        // Flag to optimize (stop if no swaps made)
        int swapped = 0;

        for (int j = 0; j < size - i - 1; j++) {
            if (arr[j] > arr[j + 1]) {
                // Swap elements
                int temp = arr[j];
                arr[j] = arr[j + 1];
                arr[j + 1] = temp;
                swapped = 1;
            }
        }

        // If no swaps made, array is sorted
        if (!swapped) {
            break;
        }
    }
}

    for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
        result *= i;
    }

    return result;
}

docs.text:
By the end of this lab, you'll be able to:

docs.title: The Problem: Repetitive Code
docs.text:
Without functions:

// Calculate area of circle 1
float area1 = 3.14159 * radius1 * radius1;

// Calculate area of circle 2
float area2 = 3.14159 * radius2 * radius2;

// Calculate area of circle 3
float area3 = 3.14159 * radius3 * radius3;

// ... repeated 100 times!

Problems:

  • Repetitive code
  • Hard to maintain (change formula everywhere)
  • Error-prone (typo in one place)
  • Difficult to test
  • Not scalable

docs.title: The Solution: Functions
docs.text:
float circleArea(float radius) {
    return 3.14159 * radius * radius;
}

// Use it
float area1 = circleArea(radius1);
float area2 = circleArea(radius2);
float area3 = circleArea(radius3);

Benefits:

  • ✅ Write once, use many times
  • ✅ Change in one place
  • ✅ Easy to test
  • ✅ Readable code
  • ✅ Reusable across projects

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A function is a self-contained block of code that:

  1. Has a name
  2. Can receive inputs (parameters)
  3. Performs a specific task
  4. Can return a result

docs.title: Anatomy of a Function
docs.text:
returnType functionName(parameterType1 param1, parameterType2 param2) {
    // Function body
    // Statements
    return value;  // Optional
}

Parts:

  • Return type — What type of value it returns (or void for none)
  • Function name — Identifier to call it
  • Parameters — Input values (optional)
  • Function body — Code to execute
  • Return statement — Value to send back (if not void)

docs.title: Declaration (Prototype)
docs.text:
Tells compiler function exists: c float circleArea(float radius); // Declaration only

Where: Usually at top of file or in header (.h)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Actual implementation:

float circleArea(float radius) {  // Definition
    return 3.14159 * radius * radius;
}

Where: Can be anywhere after declaration

docs.title: Complete Example
docs.text:
#include <stdio.h>

// Declaration (prototype)
int add(int a, int b);

int main() {
    int result = add(5, 3);
    printf("Result: %d\n", result);
    return 0;
}

// Definition
int add(int a, int b) {
    return a + b;
}

Why separate? Allows functions to call each other regardless of order!

docs.title: 1. Functions with Return Value
docs.text:
int square(int x) {
    return x * x;
}

// Usage
int result = square(5);  // result = 25

docs.title: 2. Void Functions (Procedures)
docs.text:
void printMessage(char message[]) {
    printf("%s\n", message);
    // No return statement
}

// Usage
printMessage("Hello!");  // Prints, returns nothing

docs.title: 3. Functions with No Parameters
docs.text:
int getRandomNumber() {
    return 42;  // Always returns 42 (joke!)
}

// Usage
int num = getRandomNumber();
### 4. Functions with Multiple Parameters

int max(int a, int b, int c) {
    int maximum = a;
    if (b > maximum) maximum = b;
    if (c > maximum) maximum = c;
    return maximum;
}

// Usage
int largest = max(10, 25, 18);  // 25
---

docs.title: Terminology
docs.text:
Parameters: Variables in function definition (formal parameters) 

int add(int x, int y) {  // x and y are parameters
    return x + y;
}

Arguments: Actual values passed when calling (actual parameters) 

int result = add(5, 3);  // 5 and 3 are arguments

docs.title: Parameter Passing
docs.text:
When function is called: 1. Arguments are evaluated 2. Values copied to parameters 3. Function executes with parameter values 4. Function returns (parameters destroyed) 

int main() {
    int a = 5, b = 3;
    int sum = add(a, b);  // a and b copied to parameters
    // a and b unchanged in main
}

docs.title: Default in C
docs.text:
All basic types passed by value — function receives a copy.

void increment(int x) {
    x = x + 1;
    printf("Inside function: %d\n", x);  // 6
}

int main() {
    int num = 5;
    increment(num);
    printf("In main: %d\n", num);  // Still 5!
    return 0;
}

What happens: 1. num (5) is copied to parameter x 2. x is incremented to 6 (copy modified) 3. Function ends, x destroyed 4. num in main unchanged

docs.title: Visualization
docs.text: main(): increment(): ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐ │ num │ copy → │ x │ │ 5 │ │ 6 │ └──────┘ └──────┘ ← destroyed after function

docs.title: Modifying Original Variables
docs.text:
Use pointers to pass address:

void increment(int *x) {  // Pointer parameter
    *x = *x + 1;  // Modify value at address
}

int main() {
    int num = 5;
    increment(&num);  // Pass address
    printf("%d\n", num);  // 6 (modified!)
    return 0;
}

What happens: 1. Address of num passed to function 2. Function accesses original num via pointer 3. Modifies original value 4. Change persists after function

docs.title: Visualization
docs.text: main(): ┌──────┐ │ num │ ← increment() modifies this directly │ 6 │ via pointer └──────┘

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
Pass by value (default): - Function doesn't need to modify original - Small data (int, float, char) - Want to protect original

Pass by reference (pointers): - Function needs to modify original - Large data (avoid copying) - Multiple return values needed

docs.title: Arrays Always Passed by Reference
docs.text:
Arrays are automatically passed as pointers!

void modifyArray(int arr[], int size) {
    arr[0] = 100;  // Modifies original!
}

int main() {
    int numbers[5] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
    modifyArray(numbers, 5);
    printf("%d\n", numbers[0]);  // 100 (changed!)
    return 0;
}

Why? Array name is actually a pointer to first element.

docs.title: Must Pass Size Separately
docs.text:
void printArray(int arr[], int size) {
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        printf("%d ", arr[i]);
    }
}

int main() {
    int nums[5] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};
    printArray(nums, 5);  // Must pass size!
    return 0;
}

Why? Function doesn't know array size automatically.

docs.title: Variable Scope
docs.text:
Local variables: Only accessible within function

void func() {
    int x = 10;  // Local to func
    // x only exists here
}

int main() {
    // Cannot access x from func
}

Global variables: Accessible everywhere (avoid when possible)

int globalVar = 100;  // Global

void func() {
    printf("%d", globalVar);  // Can access
}

int main() {
    printf("%d", globalVar);  // Can access
}

docs.title: Variable Lifetime
docs.text:
Automatic (local): Created when function called, destroyed when function returns

void func() {
    int x = 10;  // Created
    // ...
}  // x destroyed here

Static: Persists between function calls

void counter() {
    static int count = 0;  // Initialized once
    count++;
    printf("%d ", count);
}

int main() {
    counter();  // 1
    counter();  // 2
    counter();  // 3
    return 0;
}

docs.title: 1. Single Responsibility
docs.text:
Bad: Function does too much

void processStudent() {
    // Read input
    // Calculate average
    // Assign grade
    // Print report
    // Save to file
    // Send email
    // Too much!
}

Good: Each function has one job

float calculateAverage(int scores[], int size);
char assignGrade(float average);
void printReport(Student s);
void saveToFile(Student s);

docs.title: 2. Meaningful Names
docs.text:
Bad: 

int calc(int a, int b);  // Calc what?
void process(int x);      // Process how?

Good:

int calculateArea(int width, int height);
void validateInput(int userAge);

docs.title: 3. Keep Functions Short
docs.text: Rule of thumb: If function doesn't fit on one screen, consider splitting.

docs.title: 4. Avoid Side Effects
docs.text:
Bad: Modifies global state unexpectedly

int total = 0;  // Global

int add(int a, int b) {
    total += a + b;  // Side effect!
    return a + b;
}

Good: Pure function (no side effects)

int add(int a, int b) {
    return a + b;  // Only returns result
}

docs.title: Pattern 1: Validation Functions
docs.text:
int isValidAge(int age) {
    return (age >= 0 && age <= 120);
}

int isLeapYear(int year) {
    return (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || 
           (year % 400 == 0);
}

Returns: 1 (true) or 0 (false)

docs.title: Pattern 2: Conversion Functions
docs.text:
float celsiusToFahrenheit(float celsius) {
    return (celsius * 9.0 / 5.0) + 32.0;
}

int stringToInt(char str[]) {
    // Convert string to integer
}

docs.title: Pattern 3: Calculation Functions
docs.text:
float calculateBMI(float weight, float height) {
    return weight / (height * height);
}

float calculateCompoundInterest(float principal, 
                                 float rate, 
                                 int years) {
    return principal * pow(1 + rate, years);
}

docs.title: Pattern 4: Search/Find Functions
docs.text:
int findMax(int arr[], int size) {
    int max = arr[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < size; i++) {
        if (arr[i] > max) {
            max = arr[i];
        }
    }
    return max;
}

int linearSearch(int arr[], int size, int target) {
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        if (arr[i] == target) {
            return i;  // Return index
        }
    }
    return -1;  // Not found
}

docs.title: 1. Missing Return Statement
docs.text:
int square(int x) {
    int result = x * x;
    // Forgot return!
}  // Undefined behavior

Fix:

int square(int x) {
    return x * x;
}

docs.title: 2. Wrong Return Type
docs.text:
int divide(int a, int b) {
    return a / b;  // Integer division!
}

divide(5, 2);  // Returns 2, not 2.5

Fix:

float divide(int a, int b) {
    return (float)a / b;  // 2.5
}

docs.title: 3. Modifying Array Without Intent
docs.text:
void printArray(int arr[], int size) {
    arr[0] = 999;  // Oops! Modified original
    // ...
}

Fix: Use const if read-only

void printArray(const int arr[], int size) {
    // arr[0] = 999;  // Compiler error!
    // ...
}

docs.title: 4. Infinite Recursion
docs.text:
int bad(int n) {
    return n + bad(n - 1);  // No base case!
}

Fix: Always have base case

int good(int n) {
    if (n == 0) return 0;  // Base case
    return n + good(n - 1);
}

docs.title: 5. Not Passing Size for Arrays
docs.text:
void process(int arr[]) {
    // How many elements? Unknown!
}

Fix:

void process(int arr[], int size) {
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        // ...
    }
}

docs.title: Breaking Programs into Functions
docs.text:
Bad: Monolithic main()

int main() {
    // 200 lines of code
    // Everything in main
    // Hard to understand
    // Hard to test
    // Hard to reuse
}
Good: Modular

void displayMenu();
int getUserChoice();
void processChoice(int choice);
void displayResults();

int main() {
    displayMenu();
    int choice = getUserChoice();
    processChoice(choice);
    displayResults();
    return 0;
}

Benefits:

  • Each function small and focused
  • Easy to test individually
  • Easy to understand
  • Reusable components

docs.title: Strategies
docs.text:
1. Add Debug Prints

int factorial(int n) {
    printf("DEBUG: factorial(%d) called\n", n);

    if (n <= 1) {
        printf("DEBUG: returning 1\n");
        return 1;
    }

    int result = n * factorial(n - 1);
    printf("DEBUG: factorial(%d) = %d\n", n, result);
    return result;
}

2. Test with Simple Inputs

// Test edge cases
factorial(0);   // Should return 1
factorial(1);   // Should return 1
factorial(5);   // Should return 120

3. Verify Parameters

docs.title:
float divide(float a, float b) {
    if (b == 0) {
        printf("ERROR: Division by zero!\n");
        return 0;
    }
    return a / b;
}
Key Concepts
docs.text:
Functions encapsulate reusable code Write once, use many times Easier to maintain and test

Pass by value vs pass by reference Value: Copy of data (default) Reference: Via pointers (for modification)

Arrays always passed by reference Array name is pointer Always pass size separately

Recursion = function calling itself Must have base case Useful for tree/graph problems

Good design principles Single responsibility Meaningful names Keep functions short Avoid side effects

Scope and lifetime Local variables destroyed after function Static variables persist Minimize global variables
